WHERE THE QUESTIONS STARTED

small objects.
real cameras.
unexpected shortcuts.

In industry, I investigate driver-state recognition from roadside-camera imagery. The challenge brings together small visual cues, changing camera conditions, and a compact model that must run on an edge device.

Rendered training images give us control over the scene. They also create opportunities for a model to learn the wrong distinction. The studies below trace how we investigated that problem.

selected research studies

ONE PROGRAMME / THREE QUESTIONS

Industrial work, currently unpublished. These summaries describe the questions and qualitative findings; internal images, datasets, and numerical results are not included in this draft.

01 / GENERATOR-INDUCED SHORTCUTSObserved · limited replication

when the training data
teaches the wrong lesson.

Could the generator make pose or an object in the hand a substitute for recognizing the phone?

We compared synthetic training sets with different distractor content while matching dataset size and class balance. Removing the correlation improved real-camera recall in the documented comparison. A separate study tested using phone-positive poses for empty-handed negatives.

WHAT I TAKE FROM IT

The generator’s class structure deserves the same scrutiny as the model’s architecture.

A SHORTCUT, ILLUSTRATED
phone-positive
phone-negative
different objects + different class frequencies
a convenient correlation
can become the decision rule.

Conceptual illustration; not experiment imagery.

design, limitations & my contribution+

Experiment

Compare distractor-containing and distractor-free subsets at matched crop count and label ratio. Treat pose mirroring as a separate intervention; inspect recall as well as false alarms.

What remains uncertain

The headline comparisons have one training seed. Some precede an augmentation correction, and mirror composition is not perfectly matched. They support a shortcut hypothesis without isolating every possible explanation.

My contribution

I raised the distractor hypothesis, set priorities, and challenged comparisons. The team and coding agents implemented and scored the experiments.

02 / TESTING THE EXPERIMENT ITSELFControlled diagnostic

is it seeing the phone,
or everything around it?

If we remove the object, does the prediction change more than when we edit a matched region nearby?

We tested object-region inpainting against controls around the phone, wrist, and background. On correctly classified real examples, editing the phone changed predictions much more often than the matched surrounding region.

THE USEFUL SURPRISE

A grey mask can preserve a phone-shaped cue. How we remove the object changes what the experiment can tell us.

COMPARE THE INTERVENTIONS

Edit the phone region and ask whether the prediction changes.

Conceptual illustration; controls are essential to interpretation.

design, limitations & my contribution+

Experiment

Use inpainting to remove the phone silhouette. Compare with area-matched nearby edits and displaced/background controls; check whether mask choice changes the conclusion.

What remains uncertain

The study conditions on correctly classified positives. It does not explain every missed phone. Image edits can introduce artifacts, so a prediction change is evidence of sensitivity rather than complete causal isolation.

My contribution

I directed the broader failure investigation and used the findings to choose subsequent data experiments. Coding agents developed the diagnostic and computed the comparisons.

03 / SYNTHETIC-TO-REAL DRIFTObserved · mechanism open

better in simulation.
worse at the camera.

What does continued synthetic fine-tuning improve—and what does it forget?

A foundation-model teacher improved on synthetic validation while its real-camera performance declined. We investigated backbone adaptation, label ambiguity, and particular slices of the generated data.

THE OPEN QUESTION

How can we detect harmful adaptation before synthetic validation tells us to keep training?

THE DIRECTION OF THE FINDING
synthetic validationreal-camera evaluation

Schematic trend, not a measured performance chart.

design, limitations & my contribution+

Experiment

Compare checkpoints on synthetic and real data. Test a frozen-backbone arm and inspect label ambiguity with blinded reviews. Try selected data edits rather than assuming a correlated slice causes drift.

What remains uncertain

The run has one seed and a documented schedule bug. Several data edits did not resolve the decline. Early checkpoints were inspected on repeatedly used camera sets; a sealed test is needed for a generalization claim.

My contribution

I proposed backbone and label explanations, extended the teacher-distillation direction, and requested comparisons. Agents implemented training, attribution, and review tooling.

how I approach a research problem

MEASURE / QUESTION / REVISE

a good result should
survive a better question.

Some of the most useful progress came from correcting how we measured the problem.

01

Match the comparison.

Dataset size, label ratio, training budget, and checkpoint choice can change the story. State what is held fixed and what is still confounded.

02

Look beyond one score.

Inspect curves and per-site results. Precision changes with prevalence; fewer false alarms may also mean missing more positives.

03

Audit the evidence.

Check train/evaluation overlap, augmentation provenance, label conventions, and whether the rendered intervention actually arrived.

04

Keep the null results.

Realism edits and visibility-label experiments did not reliably deliver the expected gains. A failed explanation helps define the next test.

My role in the work

I set research priorities, propose and review hypotheses, inspect examples, and audit conclusions. I work with colleagues and coding agents on implementation. I distinguish the decisions I own from the results we produced together.

questions I want to pursue in a PhD

FUTURE DIRECTIONS
FROM AN INDUSTRIAL PROBLEM TO A RESEARCH AGENDA

measure what the
generator is teaching.

I’m interested in doctoral research in the United States on synthetic data, robust visual learning, and reliable evaluation. These are questions I want to investigate, rather than claims that the current programme has resolved.

  1. 01

    Can paired scenes predict transfer?

    Compare scenes with and without the target object. Test whether a paired score selects more useful synthetic data than confidence, diversity, or random selection.

    Proposed study · training validation remains open
  2. 02

    Can we find shortcuts before training?

    Audit class-conditional scene structure and turn generator checks into interventions that generalize beyond one task.

  3. 03

    Can a small model retain better evidence?

    Study how teacher diversity and synthetic adaptation affect what a compact student learns under a deployment budget.

A LITTLE CONTEXT

an engineer who kept
asking why.

I studied mechanical engineering at NUST, then moved into computer vision. Simulation, physical constraints, and experiments remain central to how I approach learning systems.

This page is a first account of ongoing, unpublished industrial work. Supporting artifacts will be added as they become available for public release.
